The archaeology landed and is committed (`ceecf70dd`, `explorations/perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`). The answer to your three questions, in plain words.

**How the split came about.** One person, David Chase. He built operator parameters into the interpreter in the project's first year, 2007, as name substitution: an operator argument is pulled out of the instantiation's arguments and its name is written into the body. Four years later, over ten weeks from December 2011 to January 2012, he built the compiled path's version the same way: a name channel in the class name, and a single predicate that leaves operators out of the descriptor machinery. The commit that adds that predicate says only "still busted", so no design reason is on record. The descriptor base class every type's descriptor extends was written in that same run, to make the operator case work, and ended up serving every kind. Sizes got their tag in the same commit as operators and were then never touched: no channel, no exclusion. They fell into the descriptor treatment by default, not by a decision either way.

**Why operators are different.** The specification says so. An operator parameter is a compile-time name, substituted into the declaring trait's method names, and the declarations of the actual operator are "irrelevant". A size parameter is the opposite: "instantiated at runtime with numeric values", usable wherever a variable can appear. Both paths follow that for operators: nothing anywhere dispatches on, compares or type-tests an operator argument, and in the compiled descriptor factory the operator's slot is filled with a null that nothing reads. So the two kinds differ in what the run time must do with them, and unifying them would build a descriptor for a thing the language defines as having no run-time identity.

**Should we unify.** No, and not now. Nothing in either library and nothing on the microGPT path uses an operator parameter. The question goes into a ledger row with this note beside it, taken up if something on the path ever needs one. It is not a nine-step question, since the specification already answers the semantic part.

**One flag.** The worker's closing reading favours design A for sizes, on the ground that a size's one real need is value position. That weighs the wrong thing: value position costs the same under both designs, and the probes' finding was the other need, reading a size from a value's type at a dispatched call, where A fails. The specification's own words, a size is a run-time value, point the same way as the probes. That is my reading against the worker's, marked as such in FACTS, and the size ask still waits for the revised brief, which is in flight.

The revised brief landed, I reviewed it, and it is committed with the measurements (`a77ccbee1`). Nothing is in flight. The brief now reads on its own: `explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`, with the run time's descriptor machinery explained before either design is named, the walkthrough's parts folded in, and a section that answers your questions one by one with the numbers behind each.

**What the measurement says, in plain words.**

- **Load time.** The designs differ by a few kilobytes out of about 8.6 MB of classes every run loads. A makes a descriptor class per size of each generic; B makes one small holder per distinct number, shared by all generics. With one size B loads slightly more, with eight sizes slightly less. Start-up is equal within noise.
- **The hot path.** The stamped method's bytecode is identical under A and B, with the size in it as a constant. Ten million calls take the same time, and the lead flips between rounds. Bounding the loop by the constant size is no faster than reading the storage's length, because today's cost is boxing and a transaction check per local variable. The size will only pay off once `double[]` sits under the vector, and both designs carry the constant the same way.
- **Shape checks.** Once per call site at compile time, by the checker. Never at load, never in a resolved call, never per element. Only a dispatched call tests, once per arm tried, a few nanoseconds against a call that costs tens.
- **Where they differ.** Only at a dispatched call on an arm generic in a size. B reads the size's descriptor and picks the right arm. A runs the catch-all, and its fix is about 80 unbuilt lines with a second string channel.

**The ask, as before.** Design B: a size gets the same descriptor object a type argument has, filling the slot the team's code generator already reserved. What it produces, touches, costs and commits you to is in my earlier message and in the brief's § 9 rule text. Two small probes come before the rung either way: a variant of B that makes the number's descriptor without a holder class, and the inner product's shared size. its static type.
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.

The exclusion relation is a symmetric relation between two types
whose intersection is \TYP{BottomType}.
(see \chaprefs{traits}{objects}).
It is an \emph{object trait type}
if it is defined by an object declaration.

There is a special trait type \Object, 
which is a supertype of 
every trait type, arrow type and function type, 
and of \Bottom.
\Object excludes \Void\ and every tuple type, 
and is a subtype of \Any.
\note{Should \Object\ be a trait type, or its own special type?}
``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}'' clause (described in
\secref{absorbing-units}).
If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' clause.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave such a type
parameter the implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}''.
\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples and \TYP{()} among them, which \TYP{Object}
does not (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012); \library\ are
written under \TYP{Any}, instantiating such parameters at tuple types, and the
interpreter reads the bound so.
The type group's paper of 2019 says the same: ``By default, each type parameter
has an upper bound Any'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019).
The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a
divergence that lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the
interpreter's library.}

You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.
- The type `Object` is the supertype of every value those declarations make.
- There are no Java-style primitives at the language level. `ZZ32`, `RR64` and `String` are all under `Object`. The unboxed `double` is only how the compiler may store an `RR64`.

**What `Any` has that `Object` doesn't:** tuples like `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`, functions like `ZZ32 -> ZZ32`, and the empty tuple `()`. In Fortress these are not objects. The 2012 Types chapter says the same: `Any` is the top, and `Object` excludes function types.

**Why `Any` isn't just the status quo:**
- The library's own design needs it. A two-dimensional array is indexed by a pair: `Array[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`. A list of pairs is `List[\(K, V)\]`. Under `Object`, every generic container instantiated at a tuple would be refused. That was measured at 163 refusals, most of them tuple index types, including the arrays microGPT uses.
- The draft's sentence saying `Object` dates from 2008 to 2010, before the library instantiated generics at tuples everywhere. The 2012 Types chapter makes `Any` the top.
- The compile path currently writes `Object` for an empty bound (row 412), which is why it refuses generics at tuple types today. That divergence goes away at the switch-over.

So the choice is between the draft's 2008 wording and what the library needs and the designers' later text says. Option 1 writes `Any` into the specification with a callout recording that the draft said `Object`.

POPL 2019 keeps the rule for invariant traits, allows two instantiations only when a single minimal ancestor exists (a cousin of the forest rule, for covariant traits), keeps specialisation by checking the return type at run time (the option Naden rejected), and has no self types and no numeric tower. The route ask.

**What we decide.** Which route the compiled checker takes on the rule that no type may be two applications of one generic, the rule about 60 of the library's 103 errors come from. Route A keeps the rule and flattens the tower. Route C keeps the tower and softens the rule as the patents describe.

**What A does, in three pieces of work.**

- **The interpreter learns coercion.** The specification lets a wider type declare a `coerce` that converts a narrower value when nothing else fits. The compiled path has this, the interpreter does not. The rung adds it at the interpreter's dispatch, about 150 to 200 lines in six Java files. This is batch 4's first rung, it depends on nothing, and it changes nothing for programs that run today.
- **The library's tower is flattened,** as Steele flattened the compiler prelude in 2011. ZZ32 stops being a ZZ64, ZZ64 stops being a ZZ, the integers stop being QQ, QQ stops being RR64. They become siblings under Number, each carrying its own algebra, and Number loses its catch-all operators. A `coerce` on each wider type converts from the narrower one. Fourteen headers change in the library. The sites that rely on the subtyping today, 160 in the library, 207 in the tests, 37 in microGPT, keep their text and rely on coercion instead. That is read, not yet run, and it is a rung of the batch after this one, because it needs the interpreter's coercion in place first.
- **The specification is revised** where it allows a type to extend two applications, with a decision record that preserves the original text, the reasoning and route C. A rung of batch 4, flagged as an original-tree edit, the frozen copy untouched.

**What it produces.** The checker count on the flat library goes from 103 to 22, measured on a copy. The two paths agree on the tower. Every type keeps its own specialised body, since the rule stays as the type group left it.

**What it touches.** The interpreter's dispatch, the two library files, the specification's prose, and the outputs of the interpreter tests, which are re-measured. No checker change and nothing in the compiler prelude.

**What a yes commits you to.** The tower shape changes for good, reversible only at the corrected cost from the last message. The interpreter makes its coercion choice at run time where the specification's is static, on a path whose speed does not count. And one open item comes to you before it is built: the library's `SUM` runs today on Number's catch-all with an empty sum of zero, and its replacement under A is open. If any replacement would touch a line of C4, you see the diff first, as your rule says.

**What a no costs.** Full C is blocked behind the checker overflow, with no scope for that fix, and needs the code generator's forwarding method, interpreter work and seven library declarations on top. Its count is 37, not 22. C-lite avoids the overflow but loses the specialised bodies in the middle of the tower.

**Your three questions on interpreter coercion.** Can it run first: yes, it is batch 4's first rung. Does it happen in the class loader: no. On the compiled path the checker inserts the conversion at compile time, so the bytecode carries a plain call. On the interpreter it is a choice made at dispatch in the evaluator. Will the JIT remove the overhead: on the compiled path there is only a plain conversion call, which the JIT inlines like any other, and the interpreter's cost does not count by your own rule. Your question (1), ℤ inside ℚ by coercion: under A, yes.

My recommendation: route A.

Now the next decision. The full judgement is on the page: https://claude.ai/artifact/QacjMrh2u5BfnihHkA4pPg

**How should the checker treat `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, the last early error in the library's main api?**

- **Refresher.** `trait T comprises { A, B }` closes `T`: `A` and `B` are the only types directly under it. The design has this so that two closed families with no shared member exclude each other, which lets one operator be overloaded on both.
- **The shape.** `AnyIntegral` means "some integer type" and lists the five integer types. Between it and them sits `Integral[\I\]`, the generic trait each integer type implements at itself. It isn't listed, and being generic it can't be. The checker wants every direct child listed, so it refuses the clause.
- **What the designers said.** The 2008 specification and the checker's 2009 rule say every child must be listed. The type group's 2012 texts (the later Types chapter and Welterweight) say a clause only fixes where a trait's values come from, and a trait in between adds none. By your decisions of 09-23 and 09-26, the 2012 texts weigh more, and by them the clause is right as written.
- **The library's own device** (an open marker with `excludes`) is blocked: walk then refuses the library's generic scalar operators.
- **Walk runs fine today.** Both microGPT checks pass 40 of 40 with the clause as it stands.

**Options:**
1. **Teach the checker the 2012 reading.** A generic child of a closed trait is accepted when every type the checker sees under it is listed. This is the narrow form you approved and parked on 09-21: 14 lines of Scala, no team test changes, walk untouched, one S1 note in the specification. The count stage rises from 22 to 87, because the api's hidden overloading errors become visible.
2. **The compiler library's spelling, `Integral[\I\] comprises I`.** The checker accepts it as it stands. Walk overflows its stack on it, so this needs a 6-line interpreter edit, and the interpreter tests haven't been run on it. It would be the library's first self type.

4. **Leave it.** The api's overloading errors stay hidden, and the same choice comes back at the switch-over.

**A yes to 1** means one small batch of two rungs (checker and specification) between 7R and N. It adds one ledger row for a gap that every option except the team's 2008 clause shares: an integer type that a program declares itself, in another file, isn't caught.

**A no** leaves batch 7b's overloading rung without the count of the api's errors, and brings this choice back at the switch-over.

Recommendation: option 1.

**Answer 9: the spec's rule on overloads that differ in their type parameters**
- **The rule.** Overloads of one name may not differ in their static parameters: the `[\T\]` or `[\nat n\]` list on a declaration (`basic/overloading.tex:100-107`). So a generic `f[\T\](x: T)` beside a plain `f(x: ZZ32)` would be illegal.
- **What's true today:**
  - Neither path has ever enforced it. The interpreter has accepted such pairs since 2007, and the library uses them freely.
  - The compiler's checker follows the team's 2011 paper instead. That paper was written for exactly this case: it compares overloads by their parameter types, with the type parameters folded in.
  - The rule is 2009 text. It replaced the 1.0 text of 2008, which itself said it "may be replaced when the static type checker is implemented", and the team's 2012 restart dropped it.
  - Enforcing it would refuse at least 179 pairs in the library, including the number tower's own methods.

content.content:
### The one rule, and why there is no contradiction

- The rule: **a conversion is applied to make a call possible; it never changes which body runs when a body already fits.**
- Answer 8 obeys it. Choosing `ZZ64` over `Number` inside one generic does not change which body runs. It is the same body, stamped at a narrower type. So the designers' order and your answer 8 are one rule at two levels: first the declaration (the body), by the designers' order; then the instance (the type the body is stamped at), by promotion.
- On your fork: does the generic fit as it is? Yes, on its declared types, with `T = Number`. It is more specific than the catch-all, so it is chosen. Then promotion stamps it at `ZZ64` and converts the `ZZ32`. That is your option 2, in the form the soundness check found sound ("reading A", the note's way 2).
- What it does not reach: a generic with a self-naming bound beside a catch-all. Such a generic does not fit mixed widths as they are, so the catch-all, which does, runs. The library has no such pair, and neither does microGPT; measured, nothing in the tests, demos or microGPT reaches the fork at all. With no catch-all beside it, a self-bound generic is promoted and converted like any other (measured, `O2FbLone`).

### Your idea, and what it becomes

- Your words: "if there is a conversion to a specific type, it should be applied. And only if all combinations are exhausted and we haven't reached a specific implementation, then we go to a plain implementation."
- Its sound form is the note's way 4: list every declaration and every instance that fits, with or without conversions; if one is more specific than all the others by the coercion chapter's own relation, run it, converting what it needs; otherwise fall back to the designers' order. It is C#'s rule.
- It gets three things right. It treats generic and plain arms alike. It makes answer 8 a special case. It reaches the self-bound generics.
- I recommend against it, for five reasons.
  - It treats a conversion as free. On the JVM a conversion is work: a new `ZZ64` object made from a `ZZ32`, a big-number rational made from an integer. Way 4 adds a conversion to every call where a converted arm outranks an arm that fits as it is. The designers' order never converts when an arm fits.
  - Most specific is not fastest. Under way 4, `z1 =/= z2` for two `ZZ32`s runs `QQ`'s `=/=`, converting both to rationals, because `QQ` is below `Any`. It stays so until a library line removes `QQ`'s redundant `=/=`. Every such shape in every future library file is a trap of the same kind.
  - The speed you want comes from the library, and the team's own compiled library shows how. It declares no `=` over `Any` or `Number`; each number type declares its own, and equality of other objects comes from `Equality[\T\] comprises T`. Under the designers' order, `z = 0` then reaches `ZZ32`'s own `=` with the numeral converted, because no catch-all fits first. Your idea at the library level is exactly that discipline: a specific arm at every type, no catch-all that fits first. At the language level it is C#'s order, and only C#'s.
  - The designers are unanimous. Their specification, their checker (Hilburn, 2009) and their compiled library all follow the designers' order; their later model (2011, 2012) is silent on conversion. Java, C++, Swift and Julia run an arm that needs no conversion before one that does; only C# ranks by the conversion's target. Your words of 09-23: "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
  - Its price. It reverses the designers' sentence for plain arms too: `f(ZZ64)` beats `f(Any)` for a `ZZ32`. Two gated tests and one planned assertion are restated. A call that runs today, rung Q's `ee(5)`, becomes a refusal. The proof appendix is rescoped. Walk needs a further condition to stay sound where a variable's declared type is wider than its value. The code generator's defect for two competing generic arms must be fixed first. And a probe of both paths comes before any batch.

### What your principle of speed buys on today's compiled path

- The generic at `ZZ64` is a stamped class called with no run-time test: a static load, one conversion, one call. The catch-all is reached through a dispatcher that looks up the arguments' types and tests them, two lookups and up to three tests, then the call. The JIT sees one type at the stamped call site and can inline it.
- Nothing is unboxed either way. The stamped class renames the type; it does not change the representation. The values stay `FZZ64` objects. That is phase 6's work, your storage decision of 09-19.
- The two arms run two different bodies the programmer wrote. Choosing an arm is not choosing between two compilations of one body.
- No timing was taken; none would decide between the ways. Interpreter speed decides nothing, by your rule of 09-19.

### Decision 1. Which order governs when conversions meet overloading

**The question.** What makes `b MAX 1` answer under walk for a `ZZ64` `b`, as `b + 1` does?

**Context.**
- The candidates are `QQ`'s `MAX` and the `MAX` that `ZZ64` inherits from the generic order traits, whose `self` is typed as the trait. You didn't contradict anything. The checker as it landed in batch N contradicts your decision, and option 1 fixes the checker.

The example: `a: V = k(NOf(1))`, with two declarations of `k`.
- `k[\T extends N\](x: T): T` is generic. It fits the argument as it is, and returns an `N`.
- `k(x: V): V` is plain. It fits only if `NOf(1)` is first converted to `V`.
- The result must go into `a: V`, and an `N` can be converted to `V`.

Your decision 1 says a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. So the generic `k` should run, and its `N` result gets converted to `V` at the assignment. Walk does exactly that.

What the landed checker does:
1. Its first attempt matches without any conversion, but it also demands that the result already be a `V`. The generic's result is an `N`, so the generic is ruled out.
2. Its second attempt allows conversions and finds `k(V)`, by converting the argument.

So the compiled program runs `k(V)` and walk runs the generic. The two paths disagree, and the compiled one goes against your rule.

Option 1 reorders the first attempt: match without conversion and without demanding the result type, keep the winner if its result can be converted to `V`, and only then try conversions. That's your rule as written. It's one checker rung, in batch 8.

That's all there is to it. The audit's section 6, item 4 says the same in four lines.

**`label` is not a goto.** It's a named block that code inside it can leave early, with a value. Rust's labelled `break` with a value and Scala's `boundary`/`break` are the nearest equivalents.

```
label search
  ...
  exit search with x   (leaves the block; the block's value is x)
  ...
end search
```

`exit` can only jump to the end of a `label` that encloses it, never anywhere else. If no `exit` runs, the block's value is its last expression.

**The expected type.** Yes, Fortress works like Scala and Swift here: a block's value is its last expression, and a function's body is that expression.
- The checker carries "the type this spot needs" down into an expression. A function body gets its declared return type, and the block passes it on to its last expression.
- This matters for one kind of function. In `fail[\T\](s: String): T`, `T` appears only in the result, so the arguments can't fix it. Only the expected type can.
- Example: in `x: ZZ32 = fail("bad")`, `T` becomes `ZZ32`.
- Where nothing is expected, `T` falls back to its bound, `Any`.

**`typecase`, and what batch 11's Q2 decided.**
- `typecase v of A => e1; B => e2 end` picks a branch by `v`'s run-time type.
- Its type is the union of its branches' types, so each branch gets the type the whole `typecase` is expected to have.
- Q2 asked whether a call inside a branch gets that expected type. The batch made it so.
- You're right that we didn't go through it in detail. You accepted Q1 to Q4 at their recommendations in one answer on 10-08, around 21:40 UTC, along with the other decisions of that evening.

**`label`, Q48(a).** It's the same idea with an early exit added: the block's type is the union of its last expression and its `exit` values. The real case is `String.fss:431`:

```
verify():() = label methodVerify
    ...checks...
    typecase baseString of
        s:CatString => do ... end
        EmptyString => fail "SubString of EmptyString"
        SubString   => fail "SubString of SubString"
    end
end methodVerify
```

`verify` is declared to return `()`. The checker passes `()` into the `typecase` branches, as batch 11 made it do, but not into a `label` body. So `fail`'s `T` becomes `Any`, and the method is refused. With (a), the `label` body gets `()`, the same as any function body would.

**(b), a call that is the argument of another call.** This one isn't just unimplemented. The text doesn't describe it: the inference chapter lists "an argument of another call" under what it doesn't describe yet. The way to build it is known, though: type the argument, choose which declaration of the outer call applies, then type the argument again against that declaration's parameter. Scala does this. So I'll take your "can we measure" as the go. Once the base build is ready, an Opus worker builds it as a trial copy of the checker and measures what it clears, what it breaks, and what it costs. If the result is clean, (b) joins batch 12's checker rung before the launch at the reset.
